podcast.body: During the recording sessions for their fourth album in Barbados, the band was characterized by extreme drug and alcohol consumption, resulting in a fleet of wrecked rental cars and members frequently incapacitated. "So much crack and so much heroin was consumed while the Mondays were recording their fourth album in Barbados that they wrecked a fleet of rental cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The Happy Mondays traveled to Barbados to record at Eddie Grant's Blue Wave Studios with Tina Weymouth and Chris Frantz (Talking Heads) producing. Shaun Ryder's methadone supply (four weeks' worth in 500ml vials) was dropped and shattered at the airport before departure. In Barbados he found crack cocaine as a substitute, eventually consuming up to 30 rocks a day (at 40 cents each vs. $50 back home). Bez broke his arm in a rented Jeep accident; Ryder drove another rental car through the front of a bar; keyboardist Paul Davis wrecked three rental cars; total vehicles destroyed numbered more than ten; band members sold Eddie Grant's furniture to buy more drugs. Tony Wilson flew in to find Shaun and Bez pushing a couch down the road to trade it for crack. Only one song was fully completed; Ryder forgot to write lyrics. The project cost £400,000. The one released single, "Stinking Thinking," peaked at number 31 in the UK. Factory Records filed for bankruptcy in November 1992, six weeks after the album's release. "Four hundred thousand pounds down the drain. The most expensive indie record never made."

podcast.body: This album was a follow-up recorded in Barbados at Eddy Grant's studio, but its production was plagued with problems. Shaun Ryder was largely absent for vocals, contributing lyrics for only one song, although he typically wrote lyrics later and didn't involve himself in music composition. Despite receiving good reviews and reaching number three on the charts, it is considered the record that largely marked the end of the Madchester era and was recorded amid significant band chaos including car wreckage and drug use. "It actually got good reviews, he went to number three, it did okay, it's, out of there, I think there's 10 songs in it, there's six that are good, I think there's four that, that really laid it down."

podcast.body: This album was produced by Chris France and Tina Weymouth of Talking Heads and Tom Tom Club. "And that includes the Happy Monday's and the Yes Please album in 1992."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album, intended as a follow-up to "Pills, Thrills, and Bellyaches," was recorded at Eddie Grant's studio in Barbados. The recording sessions were chaotic, marked by members destroying "more than nine cars," drinking local rum, self-medicating with local herbs, and turning sun lounges into a crack den. Shaun Ryder's inability to provide lyrics and vocals meant the band had to record most of the music without him, only for him to typically write lyrics later. Despite these difficulties and being described as "a collection of... songs" rather than a cohesive album, it surprisingly received good reviews and reached number 3 on the charts. Bez reportedly considers it his favorite Happy Mondays album. Its release is considered to have marked the end of the Madchester era. "The Happy Mondays and Stinking Thinking, from the Yes Please album, the record that pretty much marked the end of whatever Madchester was."

podcast.body: features the song "Cowboy Dave," written in memory of Dave Rowbotham, who was found murdered in 1991. The band, also associated with Factory Records, dedicated the song to their fellow Manchester musician. "The following year, the Happy Mondays, another factory band, wrote a song about Dave for their Yes Please album. It's called Cowboy Dave."
